title: Genesis 22. The Cup of Testing.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 22. The Cup of Testing.
After these things, God tested Abraham.
The words fall without warning.
After the feast.
After the weaning.
After Ishmael was sent away.
After the well in the wilderness.
After Beersheba.
After the tamarisk tree.
After El Olam.
After everything that was given and everything that was taken,
after these things, God speaks.
Abraham.
Here I am.
Take your son.
Your only son.
Whom you love.
Isaac.
And go to the land of Moriah.
Offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains I will show you.
Each word lands like a stone dropped into still water.
Your son.
Your only son.
Whom you love.
Isaac.
The accumulation is not redundant, it is surgical.
God names every layer of Abraham's attachment before He asks for it back.
Your son, the one I gave you.
Your only son, the one who replaced Ishmael.
Whom you love, the affection that binds you.
Isaac, the laughter, the promise, the covenant, the set time,
the son of a hundred-year-old man and a ninety-year-old woman.
Take him.
And offer him.
The Cup of promise, held for twenty-five years of barrenness,
born through laughter, sealed in flesh, celebrated at a weaning feast,
is now asked back.
God demands the return of the gift.
Not because He needs the boy.
Because the test is whether Abraham's hand is open or closed.
Whether the Cup is held loosely enough to be given back to the One who filled it.
Abraham rises early in the morning.
He does not argue.
He does not intercede.
He does not bargain.
The man who bargained with God for Sodom, fifty, forty-five, forty, thirty,
twenty, ten, does not speak a word.
He saddles his donkey.
He takes two young men.
He takes Isaac his son.
He splits wood for the burnt offering.
He rises and goes to the place God told him.
On the third day,
Abraham lifts up his eyes and sees the place far off.
Three days.
The same interval between the covenant-cutting in chapter fifteen and the smoking firepot.
Three days of walking with the son he is carrying to kill.
Three days of splitting wood that will burn his own flesh.
Three days of silence between God's command and the mountain.
Abraham says to the young men: Stay here with the donkey.
The boy and I will go over there and worship and come back to you.
We will come back to you.
The word is plural.
The boy and I.
Both.
Together.
The father who was told to offer his son as a burnt offering says:
We will come back.
He does not know how.
But he says it.
Abraham takes the wood of the burnt offering and lays it on Isaac his son.
He takes the fire in his hand and the knife.
They both go together.
The son carries the wood.
The father carries the fire and the knife.
The same Isaac who was carried in Sarah's arms now carries the wood that will be his pyre.
The same father who circumcised him at eight days now holds the blade that will end him.
The Cup of promise walks up a mountain carrying the wood of his own offering.
Isaac speaks: My father.
Here I am, my son.
Here is the fire and the wood.
But where is the lamb for the burnt offering?
The boy asks the question the father cannot answer.
The son who carries the wood does not know he is the lamb.
The same question that hangs over the entire chapter,
where is the lamb?
is asked by the one who will be the answer if no other appears.
Abraham says:
God will provide for Himself the lamb for a burnt offering,
my son.
God will provide.
He will see.
The same verb used when God saw Noah in chapter six.
The same verb Hagar used when she named God El Roi,
the God who sees me.
Here it becomes: God will see to it.
God will provide.
The father does not say: there is no lamb.
He does not say: you are the lamb.
He says: God will see.
And they both went together.
They came to the place God had told him.
Abraham built the altar there.
He laid the wood in order.
He bound Isaac his son.
He laid him on the altar, on the wood.
The father who was told to go, go from your country,
your kindred, your father's house,
now goes up a mountain with his son.
The altar that Noah built after the flood is rebuilt here.
The wood that was split on the first day is arranged on the stones.
The boy who carried it is bound and placed on top.
Abraham stretched out his hand and took the knife to kill his son.
The hand that was closed around the knife.
The same hand that was open when he gave Lot the choice.
The same hand that refused Sodom's wealth.
The same hand that received bread and wine from Melchizedek.
The same hand that was sealed with circumcision.
The hand that held the promise now holds the blade over the promise.
The Cup is about to be emptied by the One who filled it.
The Angel of the Lord called to him from heaven: Abraham!
Abraham!
Here I am.
Do not lay your hand on the boy.
Do not do anything to him.
For now I know that you fear God,
seeing you have not withheld your son, your only son, from Me.
The hand is stopped.
The voice comes from heaven,
the same heaven the tower of Babel tried to reach.
The same heaven from which God came down to see the city.
The same heaven from which fire fell on Sodom.
From that heaven, a voice says: Stop.
Now I know.
The test is complete.
The Cup that was given, demanded back, and offered, has been returned.
Not taken by God.
Offered by Abraham.
The hand was open.
The knife was raised.
The son was bound.
And the voice said: enough.
The fear of God has been witnessed.
Not in what Abraham said.
Not in what he felt.
In what his hand was about to do.
Abraham lifts up his eyes and looks.
Behind him, a ram.
Caught in a thicket by its horns.
Abraham lifts his eyes and sees the ram caught in the thicket.
The substitute is there when he looks,
but the text does not tell when or how it came there.
The God who stops Abraham provides the ram on the mountain.
The Cup is not emptied.
The test exposes whether the hand that holds the promise can release it back to the One who gave it.
Abraham went and took the ram and offered it up as a burnt offering instead of his son.
Instead of his son.
The first substitution in Scripture.
The ram in place of Isaac.
The animal caught by its horns, the head, the strength,
caught in thorns.
The offering that was not the son but stood in the son's place.
Abraham called the name of that place: The Lord Will Provide.
the mountain of the Lord it shall be provided.
Yahweh Yireh.
On The place where the promise nearly died is named for the God who provided.
The place where the knife was raised is named for the God who stopped it.
The mountain where a father bound his son is named for the God who gave a ram.
The Cup of testing is not about God taking.
It is about whether the vessel will hold the Cup with an open hand.
And on the mountain where the hand was opened,
the Cup was returned, fuller than before.
The Angel of the Lord called to Abraham a second time from heaven:
By Myself I have sworn, says the Lord.
Because you have done this thing and have not withheld your son,
your only son, I will surely bless you.
I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand on the seashore.
Your offspring shall possess the gate of his enemies.
And in your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed,
because you have obeyed My voice.
God swears by Himself.
The same God who walked alone through the pieces in chapter fifteen now speaks alone from heaven.
The covenant that was cut in blood is now sealed by oath.
The promise that was given by calling, confirmed by stars,
sealed in flesh, endangered by fear, filled at the set time,
is now sworn by the name of God Himself because you have not withheld.
Because you obeyed.
The Cup is not fuller because the son was nearly killed.
It is fuller because the father's hand was open.
The promise that was given to a man who grabbed for safety is now sealed upon a man who released what he loved most.
The vessel that fumbled in Egypt, that arranged in Hagar,
that lied in Gerar, has now, on a mountain in Moriah,
opened its hand.
And the Cup that was returned is sealed by an oath that depends on no one but God.
Abraham returned to his young men.
They rose and went together to Beersheba.
Abraham lived at Beersheba.
Together.
Twice on the mountain Genesis says they went together.
After the offering, Genesis names Abraham returning to the young men;
Isaac is not named in that sentence.
The promise continues, but the descent itself is left strangely spare.
The Cup is not emptied.
What looked like the end has become continuation.
After these things, Abraham was told:
Milcah has also borne children to your brother Nahor.
Uz, Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel.
Bethuel fathered Rebekah.
A name appears at the end of the chapter where a son was nearly sacrificed.
Rebekah.
The woman who will carry the next generation is named at the bottom of the mountain where the current generation was nearly ended.
The Cup that was tested and returned already contains the next vessel.
The promise does not stop at Isaac.
It reaches forward, through a brother's wife, through a niece,
through a woman who has not yet been seen,
toward a future the mountain did not take.
The Cup of testing holds.
The ram was there when Abraham looked.
The oath is sworn.
The next generation is named.
What looked like the end becomes a seal.
